title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals and Threats

sources.title: 2026-2027 FBLA Cybersecurity Guidelines
sources.scope: Read study guide pages 5-6 for current scope and wording of assigned Security Fundamentals and Cyber Threats and Vulnerabilities objectives; used only to establish scope, not technical mechanisms.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63A-4: Identity Proofing and Enrollment
sources.scope: Read identity proofing overview and passages on resolution, evidence/attribute validation, verification of rightful owner, enrollment, and assurance limits.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.scope: Read authentication definition, AAL summaries, distinct-factor MFA, authenticator control, phishing resistance, OTP and out-of-band limitations.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Attestation
sources.scope: Read definition: digitally sign hardware-secured measurements and have requester validate signature and measurements; glossary term context is SP 1800-19B.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Honeypot
sources.scope: Read definition of an attractive system/resource for potential intruders. NIST glossary term identifies resource examples, not a complete taxonomy of honeynet or honeyfile.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture
sources.scope: Read official abstract: no implicit trust based solely on physical/network location; ZTA focuses on users, assets, and resources. Full publication not read.

sources.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.scope: Read SQL injection mechanism, parameterized query, allow-list structural choices, and least-privilege passages.

sources.title: CISA: Understanding Denial-of-Service Attacks
sources.scope: Read DoS flood and SYN-flood mechanics, botnet-based DDoS, compromised devices as victims, monitoring, and response. Page is explicitly archived/outdated; use for basic mechanism only.

sources.title: RFC 9325: Recommendations for Secure Use of TLS/DTLS
sources.scope: Read TLS version/fallback guidance: TLS 1.2 clients must not fall back to earlier deprecated versions; document recommends modern secure deployment and notes guidance is point-in-time.

sources.title: RFC 6962: Certificate Transparency
sources.scope: Read hash-tree definitions: SHA-256 digests, distinct leaf/node prefixes for second-preimage resistance, and proof construction. Does not state birthday bound; used for hash/digest context only.

sheets.title: Security Goals, Trust, and Number Bases

pages.title: CIA and Zero Trust
notes: Confidentiality limits data reading to authorized parties.
Integrity resists unauthorized change or destruction.
Availability gives authorized users timely access.
Encryption supports confidentiality, not data truth.
Audit controls can expose changes; logs need protection.
Tested backups support recovery and availability.
Zero Trust gives no trust from location alone.
Evaluate user, device, resource, and context per request.
Example: verify worker and device before payroll access.

pages.title: Identity, Attestation, and AAA
notes: Proofing links a claimed identity to a real person.
Resolution finds a unique identity in the served population.
Validation checks evidence and attribute facts.
Verification checks applicant is rightful evidence owner.
Authentication later checks control of a bound authenticator.
Attestation signs hardware-secured measurements for review.
Attestation describes device measurements, not human identity.
Trust depends on keys, measurements, and verifier policy.
AAA: authentication, authorization, and accounting.
Authorization permits actions; accounting records activity.

pages.title: Nonrepudiation and Least Privilege
notes: Nonrepudiation seeks evidence resisting denial of an action.
A signature alone cannot prove who controlled its key.
Identity binding, key custody, intent, and time matter.
Legal and system assumptions bound attribution claims.
Least privilege grants only necessary resource/action rights.
Use narrow roles and time-bound elevation where feasible.
Review grants; revoke access when duties or roles change.
It limits blast radius, not all misuse or compromise.
OWASP says least DB privilege limits injection damage.

pages.title: Binary, Decimal, and Hex
notes: Binary is base 2; decimal is base 10; hex is base 16.
Hex digits are 0-9 and A-F; A-F represent values 10-15.
Place values are powers of the base, right to left.
Binary 1011 equals decimal 8+2+1, or 11.
Hex 2F equals decimal 2*16+15, or 47.
Four binary bits form one hex digit: 1011 becomes B.
Pad on left: 11010 becomes 0001 1010, or hex 1A.
A byte is 8 bits; two hex digits display one byte.
Hex displays bits compactly; it does not encrypt them.
Hashes output fixed-length digests; encoding adds no strength.

practice.prompt: A compliant laptop requests payroll access. Give a Zero Trust decision.
practice.answer: Verify user, device, and resource-specific policy; allow only the required payroll action for an appropriate session. LAN/VPN presence alone is not authorization.

practice.prompt: Convert binary 1101 to decimal and one hex digit.
practice.answer: 8+4+1=13 decimal; four bits map to hex D. Hex is a representation of the same bits, not encryption.

pages.title: Proofing, Factors, and Device Trust
notes: Proofing links a person identity at stated assurance.
It resolves, validates evidence, then verifies owner.
Authentication checks control of an account authenticator.
A device report is not user proof; login is not device proof.
Attestation signs hardware-secured measurements for review.
It depends on trusted measurement, signing key, and verifier.
Authentication shows account control, not real-world identity.
Assurance reduces risk; it does not promise certainty.
Enrollment and recovery also need secure proofing controls.

pages.title: AAA, MFA, and Zero Trust
notes: Authentication verifies control; authorization permits use.
Accounting: record relevant use for review and investigation.
MFA uses distinct types: know, have, or are.
Two passwords are both know factors, not MFA by themselves.
Password plus registered security key combines know and have.
SMS codes can be intercepted/phished; not phishing-resistant.
Zero Trust checks identity/context for each resource request.
Managed device and verified worker get payroll read access.
Network location or VPN alone does not grant implicit trust.
Device posture is a signal; it does not identify the user.

pages.title: Least Privilege
notes: Grant only resources/actions needed for assigned work.
Separate routine accounts from administrative elevation.
A reporting service may read a view, not own the database.
Use role scopes and expire temporary permissions.
Review access after job, project, or status changes.
Remove stale rights; protect service/database accounts too.
Least privilege limits harm from bugs or stolen accounts.
It does not stop every authorized misuse or compromise.
OWASP treats it as damage reduction, not injection prevention.

pages.title: Honeypots, Honeynets, and Honeyfiles
notes: NIST calls honeypot an attractive resource for intruders.
A decoy service/file can make unexpected access observable.
Honeynet commonly means connected decoy systems.
Honeyfile commonly means monitored decoy document/artifact.
No separate NIST glossary entries for these labels were found.
Access can alert defenders; decoys do not block attacks.
Isolate decoys from production; restrict outbound connections.
Use synthetic content, monitor alerts, assign response owner.
Never place real credentials or sensitive records in decoys.
Containment and safe isolation are separate design controls.

practice.prompt: Why do device attestation and identity proofing establish different facts?
practice.answer: Attestation lets a requester validate signed hardware measurements; proofing links a human claim to a real person. Keys, measurement trust, and proofing evidence each have limits.

practice.prompt: A finance analyst needs one report. Name a least-privilege grant.
practice.answer: Grant read access only to that report/view, log its use, and review or revoke when duties change; broad database administration is unnecessary risk.

pages.title: Threat Actors and Motives
notes: Insiders have organizational access; outsiders do not.
Either may act deliberately or cause harm through error.
Financial gain can motivate theft, extortion, or fraud.
Espionage seeks protected information for strategic advantage.
Data theft may support resale, fraud, or later intrusion.
Disruption or ideology may motivate service or data attacks.
Assess capability, access, opportunity, and target as well.
Motive is a hypothesis, not proof of actor identity.
Controls should address behavior and access, not stereotypes.

pages.title: Virus Varieties and Other Malware
notes: Malware is software used to harm, spy, extort, or control.
A virus attaches to a host file or boot area to spread.
File virus infects executable files when they run.
Boot-sector virus targets startup records or boot media.
Polymorphic viruses vary code/signature during replication.
Variation may evade simple signatures; behavior checks help.
Trojan masquerades as benign software to induce execution.
A worm self-propagates across systems or networks.
Logic bomb activates when a time/event condition is met.
One malware sample may combine more than one behavior.

pages.title: Vulnerabilities and Exploit Classes
notes: Vulnerability is a weakness; exploit is a way to use it.
Injection treats input as command/query syntax, not data.
Parameterized SQL separates values from query structure.
Buffer overflow writes beyond allocated memory bounds.
Race occurs when timing changes shared state unexpectedly.
Atomic operations/locks can prevent unsafe check-use races.
Jailbreaking weakens platform restrictions or sandboxing.
Backdoor is hidden access; zero-day has no effective fix yet.
Known unpatched flaws may have fixes; test and apply patches.

pages.title: Reduce Exposure
notes: Bind untrusted data; do not concatenate into SQL syntax.
Allowlist identifiers and sort choices from fixed options.
Least database privilege limits damage, not injection itself.
Use bounds-safe code and safe shared-state access.
Apply security updates after risk-appropriate testing.
Remove unused services and reduce exposed attack surface.
Limit user/service rights to reduce malware blast radius.
Backups support recovery but do not prevent infection.
Signatures can miss new or altered malware.
Use layered controls; no single tool guarantees prevention.

practice.prompt: Contrast a file virus, worm, Trojan, and logic bomb.
practice.answer: Virus attaches to a host; worm self-propagates; Trojan masquerades as legitimate; logic bomb waits for a trigger. A sample can combine behaviors.

practice.prompt: A query concatenates a submitted name into SQL. What flaw and fix?
practice.answer: This creates injection risk because input can become SQL syntax. Bind the value as a parameter; use fixed allowlists for structural choices. Binding does not grant authorization.

sheets.title: Social, Service, Cryptographic, and Wireless Threats

pages.title: Social Engineering
notes: Phishing deceives users into revealing data or unsafe action.
Spear-phishing tailors lures to a person or group.
Smishing uses SMS/text; vishing uses voice or phone calls.
Scammers impersonate banks, vendors, coworkers, or help desks.
Urgency, secrecy, payment changes, code requests warn users.
Sender display and caller ID can be spoofed.
Verify through a known independent number or contact path.
Never disclose passwords or one-time login codes to callers.
Report suspicious messages through the approved route.

pages.title: DoS and DDoS Mechanics
notes: DoS makes a service unavailable to legitimate users.
Flooding can exhaust link capacity or server request handling.
SYN flood leaves TCP handshakes incomplete, holding state.
Application requests consume CPU, memory, or worker slots.
DDoS coordinates many machines against one target.
Botnet is compromised devices under remote control.
Compromised devices are victims as well as traffic sources.
Distributed sources complicate attribution and filtering.
Traffic spikes and maintenance can mimic attack symptoms.
Monitor traffic; coordinate with admin and provider.

pages.title: Hash Collisions and Birthday Effect
notes: A hash maps input data to a fixed-length digest.
Collision means distinct inputs share a finite digest.
Preimage seeks input for a chosen digest: a different goal.
For ideal n-bit hash, generic collision work is about 2^(n/2).
Birthday effect finds any pair sooner than target preimage.
This is a probability/work estimate, not an exact threshold.
Collision is not decryption or original-message recovery.
Hashing differs from reversible, key-based encryption.
RFC 6962 uses domain-separated SHA-256 Merkle-tree hashes.

pages.title: Downgrades and Wireless Weaknesses
notes: Downgrade induces peers to use weaker protocol/options.
Fallback to obsolete versions can expose known weaknesses.
RFC 9325 says TLS 1.2 clients must not fall back earlier.
Use maintained protocols; compatibility can limit versions.
Evil twin imitates a trusted Wi-Fi name to lure users.
SSID display alone does not authenticate the access point.
WEP's weak IV/key design lets traffic aid key recovery.
WEP is obsolete; use modern WPA2/WPA3 configuration instead.
Hidden SSID and MAC filtering do not replace encryption.
HTTPS/VPN have limits; rogue access-point risk remains.

practice.prompt: A caller demands an SMS code and urgent payment change. Respond safely.
practice.answer: Treat as possible vishing: do not share the code or alter payment. Verify using a known contact number and report. Caller ID can be forged.

practice.prompt: Does a birthday collision attack decrypt a hashed message?
practice.answer: No. It seeks any colliding pair; ideal n-bit hash generic collision work is about 2^(n/2). It neither decrypts nor finds a chosen message's preimage.

lab.title: Safe fictional phishing and availability tabletop
steps: Read a fictional payroll voice-call scenario asking for an SMS code and bank change.
Identify vishing cues; choose independent verification and approved reporting path.
Discuss fictional service slowdown: identify resource/provider, preserve event notes, notify response lead.
Name approved mitigation options; do not generate traffic, scan, click links, or contact real numbers.
expected: No code or payment change is disclosed; callback uses a known contact route.
Participants distinguish DoS capacity exhaustion from ordinary outages and identify provider/response coordination.
No live systems, credentials, traffic, or personal logs are used.

limitations: NIST CSRC glossary provided a direct honeypot definition; separate authoritative NIST entries for honeynet and honeyfile were not found. Those common instructional distinctions are explicitly qualified.
CISA DoS article is archived and may not reflect current policy; it is used only for basic attack mechanics, while mitigation is described cautiously.
RFC 6962 supports hash/digest and Merkle-tree mechanics but not the birthday bound itself; the generic birthday estimate is standard probability analysis and is labeled as an idealized bound.
